title: The right container
description:
Each of these is easy with the right container and slow without it. The tests use 100,000-element inputs.

```cpp
int firstUnique(const std::string& s);                                           // index of the first character that occurs once, or -1
std::vector<std::string> topWords(const std::vector<std::string>& words, std::size_t k);   // the k most frequent, ties alphabetical
int longestRun(const std::vector<int>& values);                                  // the longest run of consecutive integers, in any order
bool nearbyDuplicate(const std::vector<int>& values, std::size_t k);             // two equal values at most k positions apart?
std::vector<int> slidingMedians(const std::vector<int>& values, std::size_t k);  // the median of every window of k (k is odd)
```

- `topWords` returns fewer than `k` words if there are fewer distinct words.
- `longestRun({ 100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2 })` is 4 (1, 2, 3, 4). Duplicates count once. O(n) expected.
- `nearbyDuplicate` keeps a set of the last `k` values: O(n).
- `slidingMedians`: for `{ 5, 1, 4, 2, 3 }` and `k = 3` the windows are `{5,1,4}`, `{1,4,2}`, `{4,2,3}`, so the medians are `{ 4, 2, 3 }`. Use a `std::multiset` holding the current window and an iterator to its middle, or rebuild in O(k log k) per window if you prefer (k is at most 101 in the big test).
hints: For `topWords`, count with an `unordered_map`, copy the pairs into a vector, and sort by count descending, then word ascending.

A simple correct `slidingMedians`: keep the window in a `std::multiset`; after each step take `*std::next(window.begin(), k / 2)`. That is O(k) per window, fine for k = 101. Keeping an iterator to the middle and nudging it makes it O(log k).
